items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

In a long-lived ChatGPT Work thread, the user repeatedly experienced turns making no visible progress under GPT-6 Astra. Repeated requests to continue did not reliably resume useful work. The user reports that switching to GPT-6.1 Sol restored progress. This is a user-observed correlation, not proof of a model-serving root cause.

The affected task combined connected-app retrieval, attachment materialization, local calculations and optional subagents. Private task contents and connected data are intentionally omitted.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The incident occurred in an existing long-lived Work conversation with many prior turns and subagents:
1. Continue an analysis task under GPT-6 Astra.
2. The thread stops delivering useful progress despite repeated continuation messages.
3. Switch the conversation to GPT-6.1 Sol; ordinary connected-app reads and local execution proceed.

No deterministic minimal reproduction is available yet. We cannot establish whether automatic compaction, collaboration scheduling or another host state was active at every stall.

### What is the expected behavior?

A turn should complete, expose the operation it is waiting on, or return a cancellable bounded error. A failed optional collaborator should not indefinitely block the parent thread. Switching models should not be required to recover an otherwise executable task.

### Additional information

- Surface: ChatGPT Work, managed cloud runtime. Exact client/app-server build and client OS were not exposed to the agent.
- Incident observed: 2026-10-20 through early 2026-10-21, UTC+08.
- A prior visible `collaboration.send_message` operation was aborted after approximately 278.4 seconds. This does not account for all user-reported unresponsiveness.
- An agent-authored script also raised `TypeError` while dereferencing an undefined temporary-store value. That script error is a separate workflow defect and is not asserted to be the platform root cause.
- After the model switch, two workout-data queries returned in approximately 2.24 and 2.94 seconds; six targeted heart-rate queries returned in approximately 1.60–2.50 seconds. Attachment reads, local calculations and saving completed.
- No approval prompt was observed in the visible affected operations. Client session logs and backend traces are not available in the managed runtime.
- A local workflow instruction unnecessarily required an Astra review before delivery. That dependency is being removed as a mitigation; it does not repair the host or prove the platform incident resolved.
- Potentially related, but not confirmed duplicates: #43062 (compaction), #33777 (spawn lifecycle), #32756 (message scheduling). Those reports concern specific app/CLI paths; applicability to this Work incident is unknown.

Please advise which Work diagnostic/session identifier and private channel are needed to correlate the stalled turns with backend traces. No raw conversation, account identifiers, credentials or private connected-app data are included.

Please restore the ability to manually create and configure scheduled automations in the Codex desktop app through a dedicated UI, without requiring an AI conversation.

Previously, users could manually configure automation tasks. Now, automation creation appears to depend on interacting with the AI.

**The main problem is that when a user exhausts their Codex usage quota, they can no longer create scheduled tasks, even if they only need to configure a simple schedule.**

This creates an unnecessary dependency between basic task management and AI inference quota.

**Requested improvements:**

1. Restore a manual "Create Automation" button.
2. Allow users to configure task names, instructions, working directories, schedules, and recurrence directly in the UI.
3. Allow users to edit, enable, disable, and delete automations without consuming AI conversation quota.
4. Separate automation configuration from AI task execution. AI execution can still be subject to usage limits.

Basic scheduling and task configuration should not require AI inference or available conversation quota.

Please preserve AI-assisted automation creation as an optional convenience, rather than making it the only available method.

items.title: Linux sandbox: a deny-read glob makes sandbox construction fail fatally when a directory under its root disappears during the ripgrep scan

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
**Version:** codex-cli 0.163.0 (same code in 0.160.1, and on `main` as of the 2026-10-15 change to `codex-rs/linux-sandbox/src/bwrap.rs`). Linux aarch64, bubblewrap sandbox.

### What happens

A permissions profile denies reads with a glob, e.g. `"/data/**/secret.txt" = "none"`. Bubblewrap masks only concrete paths. So before every sandbox is built, Codex expands the glob with `rg --files --hidden --no-ignore --null --glob <glob> -- <root>`, where `<root>` is the static prefix of the pattern. This happens at thread start (the AGENTS.md loader goes through the fs sandbox helper) and for every sandboxed command.

Another process may be changing files under `<root>` at the same time, as `npm ci` or Codex's own plugin installer do. Then `rg` lists a directory, the directory is removed before `rg` opens it, and `rg` exits 2 with `No such file or directory (os error 2)`. `ripgrep_files` turns any non-zero status other than "1 with empty stderr" into `CodexErr::Fatal`. So sandbox construction fails:

```
Failed to create session: failed to load AGENTS.md instructions for environment `local`: fs sandbox helper failed with status exit status: 1: error building bubblewrap command: Fatal error: ripgrep unreadable glob scan failed for <root>: rg: <root>/…/node_modules/<pkg>: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```

At thread start, the thread is never created. For a command, the command fails. A path that no longer exists cannot be read, so it needs no mask. The failure protects nothing.

### Reproduction

`repro.py` (attached) creates a temporary directory with a `secret.txt` under a denied glob and a 32k-file tree under the same root. It churns directories in that tree from a thread and runs `codex sandbox <profile> -- cat secret.txt` 60 times:

```
$ python3 repro.py 60
codex sandbox runs=60 glob_scan_max_depth=unset: 41 failed to build the sandbox, 19 ran with secret.txt denied
example: rg: /tmp/tmpt8_4dkny/data/work/node_modules/tmp1/d140: No such file or directory (os error 2)

$ python3 repro.py 60 3
codex sandbox runs=60 glob_scan_max_depth=3: 0 failed to build the sandbox, 60 ran with secret.txt denied
```

### Workaround

`glob_scan_max_depth` in the profile's `filesystem` table, as the startup warning about unbounded `**` suggests. It works only when every directory that can vanish is deeper than the cap minus one. `rg --max-depth N` still opens the directories at depth N-1. With the churn at depth 3 and a cap of 4, the same repro still fails, 3 out of 60. The cap also gives up masking matches below it.

### Suggested fix

Treat "not found" during the expansion as "nothing to mask", not as a fatal error. In `ripgrep_files`, an exit status 2 whose stderr lines are all `No such file or directory (os error 2)` can use stdout as the result. In the `glob_files` fallback, skip `NotFound` from `read_dir` and from `entry.file_type()`. Every other error can stay fatal, so deny-read never weakens silently.

<details><summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
"""Repro: a deny-read glob makes Linux sandbox construction fail when a directory under the glob's root vanishes mid-scan.

Usage: python3 repro.py [runs] [max_depth]
Needs `codex` on PATH (Linux, bubblewrap sandbox). Everything lives in a fresh temporary directory.
"""
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import threading
from pathlib import Path

runs = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 60
depth = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    root = Path(tmp) / "data"
    (root / "a" / "b").mkdir(parents=True)
    (root / "a" / "b" / "secret.txt").write_text("secret\n")
    # A large, static tree under the same root, so the scan takes long enough to race.
    big = root / "work" / "node_modules"
    for i in range(400):
        for j in range(10):
            d = big / f"p{i}" / f"s{j}"
            d.mkdir(parents=True)
            for k in range(8):
                (d / f"f{k}.js").touch()
    codex_home = Path(tmp) / "codex-home"
    codex_home.mkdir()

    filesystem = f'"{root}/**/secret.txt" = "none"'
    if depth:
        filesystem = f"glob_scan_max_depth = {depth}, " + filesystem
    args = ["-c", 'default_permissions="p"',
            "-c", f'permissions.p={{extends = ":workspace", filesystem = {{{filesystem}}}}}']

    stop = False

    def churn():
        """What `npm ci` or a plugin installer does: directories appear and vanish."""
        i = 0
        while not stop:
            p = big / f"tmp{i % 50}"
            for k in range(200):
                (p / f"d{k}" / "e").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            shutil.rmtree(p, ignore_errors=True)
            i += 1

    worker = threading.Thread(target=churn)
    worker.start()
    failures, example, denied = 0, "", 0
    try:
        for _ in range(runs):
            r = subprocess.run(["codex", "sandbox", *args, "--", "cat", str(root / "a" / "b" / "secret.txt")],
                               env={**os.environ, "CODEX_HOME": str(codex_home)}, capture_output=True, text=True,
                               timeout=120)
            if "unreadable glob scan failed" in r.stderr:
                failures += 1
                example = example or r.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1]
            elif "Permission denied" in r.stderr:
                denied += 1
    finally:
        stop = True
        worker.join()
    print(f"codex sandbox runs={runs} glob_scan_max_depth={depth or 'unset'}: "
          f"{failures} failed to build the sandbox, {denied} ran with secret.txt denied")
    if example:
        print("example:", example[:300])
```
</details>

items.title: Document a loss-reporting diagnostic export for Code Mode executions

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI 0.163.0. This request is based on static review of public source commit `83086188ae0614bd882818ff1aa23f3194962012`; no runtime reproduction or session data is attached.

### What feature would you like to see?

A documented, bounded diagnostic export for Code Mode executions that reports its own coverage and recording failures.

The pinned [rollout-trace design](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/83086188ae0614bd882818ff1aa23f3194962012/codex-rs/rollout-trace/README.md#L94) is useful and explicitly best-effort. Recorded nested dispatches have cell/call relationships and serialized runtime results. The inspected [raw event schema](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/83086188ae0614bd882818ff1aa23f3194962012/codex-rs/rollout-trace/src/raw_event.rs#L69) does not provide a dedicated complete per-execution effective `enabled_tools` snapshot. Missing events or payloads also leave uncertainty about what was recorded. Invoked-tool records cannot enumerate enabled-but-unused capabilities.

For workflows that need to compare configured capabilities with observed calls, could a supported export provide:

- Effective tool definitions for each execution, including enabled tools that were not called, and registry generation/change signals.
- Stable thread, turn, execution, cell and invocation linkage, with a documented mapping between identifiers.
- Structured inputs, actual results and errors, with the represented boundary clearly stated: serialized runtime values or original transport bytes.
- Explicit dropped, truncated, write-failure and terminal/incomplete status, so a partial capture cannot be mistaken for complete evidence.

Payload retention should be bounded and sensitive payload capture opt-in. The normal session could retain its best-effort behavior while the exported diagnostic artifact explicitly reports incomplete recording.

If an existing supported interface already meets this need, documentation of its exact coverage and compatibility with this CLI would resolve the question without a new feature.

### Additional information

Related context includes the historical, closed [#9284](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/9284) on tool-step output retention and the open [#23411](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/23411) on Code Mode hook visibility. Neither establishes the combined registry and loss-reporting export contract described here. This request contains no private logs, local paths, credentials or session output.

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.163.0

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6.1-sol. I also previously attempted to use gpt-5.6-sol.

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64 (Windows 11 x64).

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Windows PowerShell on Windows x64. No terminal multiplexer is in use.

### Codex doctor report

```json
Codex doctor --json summary:

Codex CLI: 0.163.0
Managed app-server: 0.163.0, running
Authentication: ChatGPT account; ChatGPT tokens present
Configuration: parses successfully
HTTP endpoint reachability: successful
Responses WebSocket handshake: successful
WebSocket diagnostic: server model present: false
Update status: CLI reports version 0.163.0 as current
Non-critical warnings: ignored legacy configuration setting, malformed custom agent definition, and unresolved optional MCP server path
```

### What issue are you seeing?

Summary
On Windows, using Codex CLI 0.163.0 with a ChatGPT Plus account, Sol models are missing from the resolved model catalog and the interactive /model picker. Explicitly selecting GPT-6.1 Sol through the built-in OpenAI provider fails with HTTP 400:

`{"type":"error","status":400,"error":{"type":"invalid_request_error","message":"The 'gpt-6.1-sol' model is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account."}}`

This remains reproducible after updating the CLI and restarting the managed app-server daemon.

This report is related to [#55028](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/55028), where another user reported that upgrading to 0.163.0 restored Sol model availability. My results differ: both the CLI and managed app-server report 0.163.0, but Sol models remain unavailable in my environment.

**Observed behavior**
The resolved catalog contains only these five entries:
| Model | Visibility |
| --- | --- |
| `gpt-reserve` | `hide` |
| `gpt-6-luna` | `list` |
| `gpt-5.6-terra` | `list` |
| `gpt-5.6-luna` | `list` |
| `codex-auto-review` | `hide` |

Neither `gpt-6.1-sol` nor `gpt-6-sol` appears in the resolved catalog. The `/model` picker also shows Terra and Luna but no Sol models.

In contrast, `codex debug models --bundled` lists the following Sol definitions with visibility set to list:

- gpt-6.1-sol
- gpt-6-sol
- gpt-5.6-sol

I understand that bundled definitions do not guarantee account entitlement. However, the difference between the bundled and resolved catalogs is reproducible.

**Error when explicitly selecting GPT-6.1 Sol**
The CLI displays this warning:

`Model metadata for 'gpt-6.1-sol' not found. Defaulting to fallback metadata; this can degrade performance and cause issues.`

The request is then rejected with:

The 'gpt-6.1-sol' model is `not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account`.

The full error is an HTTP 400 `invalid_request_error`.

**Troubleshooting already performed**

- Updated Codex CLI to 0.163.0.
- Confirmed the managed app-server also runs 0.163.0.
- Ran codex app-server daemon update; it reported noUpdate.
- Restarted the managed app-server daemon from a non-elevated PowerShell session.
- Retested explicit model selection after the restart.
- Ran codex doctor --json and reviewed the diagnostics locally.

None of these steps restored Sol model availability.
The doctor report confirms successful network reachability and a successful WebSocket handshake, but its WebSocket diagnostic reports `server model present: false`.

The issue therefore persists on the reported current CLI version and does not appear to be resolved by restarting the managed daemon.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

**Prerequisites**

- Windows 11 x64
- Codex CLI 0.163.0
- A ChatGPT Plus account authenticated through ChatGPT sign-in
- Built-in OpenAI provider

**Steps**

1. Sign in to Codex CLI with the ChatGPT account.
2. Run the following command to inspect the resolved catalog:

```
codex debug models | ConvertFrom-Json |
  Select-Object -ExpandProperty models |
  Select-Object slug, display_name, visibility
```

3. Verify that neither gpt-6.1-sol nor gpt-6-sol appears.
4. Inspect the bundled catalog:

```
codex debug models --bundled | ConvertFrom-Json |
  Select-Object -ExpandProperty models |
  Where-Object {
    $_.slug -match 'sol' -or $_.display_name -match 'sol'
  } |
  Select-Object slug, display_name, visibility
```

5. Verify that the bundled catalog lists gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6-sol, and gpt-5.6-sol with visibility list.
6. Open the interactive /model picker and observe that no Sol models are listed.
7. Explicitly request GPT-6.1 Sol:

`codex exec --model gpt-6.1-sol --skip-git-repo-check "Reply with exactly: OK"`

8. Observe the missing-model-metadata warning followed by HTTP 400 stating that gpt-6.1-sol is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account.
9. Restart the managed app-server daemon, repeat the test, and observe that the issue persists.

The resolved catalog, bundled catalog, and explicit-selection error can be compared using these steps.

### What is the expected behavior?

If GPT-6.1 Sol is available to my ChatGPT Plus account under the applicable rollout, I would expect it to appear in the resolved model catalog and /model picker and to accept requests through the built-in OpenAI provider.

If the model is not enabled for my account, I would expect Codex to communicate the applicable eligibility or rollout restriction clearly rather than presenting a generic unsupported-model error after explicit selection.

I am not claiming that the current evidence proves an entitlement bug or backend regression. It demonstrates a reproducible discrepancy between the bundled catalog, resolved catalog, and request acceptance in my environment.

### Additional information

**Related issue**

items.body:
### Summary

PowerShell `.ps1` scripts are rejected inside Codex's Windows MXC sandbox with `AuthorizationManager check failed`. In the same environment, Windows PowerShell 5.1 cannot read the effective execution policy from the registry (`Requested registry access is not allowed`). The same local script runs in the host PowerShell session, where the policy is `RemoteSigned`.

### Environment

- Codex CLI: `0.163.0`
- Windows 11 Pro 26H2, build `26300.9807`
- Windows PowerShell 5.1.26100.9807
- PowerShell 7.6.6 installed from Microsoft Store/MSIX
- `approval_policy = "on-request"`
- `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"`
- `[windows] sandbox = "mxc"`
- No `MachinePolicy` or `UserPolicy` execution policy is configured.

### Steps to reproduce

1. In an ordinary host Windows PowerShell session, run `Get-ExecutionPolicy` and a local test `.ps1`. The effective policy is `RemoteSigned`, and the script succeeds.
2. Run `Get-ExecutionPolicy -List` from a Windows PowerShell process launched inside Codex MXC. It fails with:

   ```text
   Get-ExecutionPolicy : Requested registry access is not allowed.
   ```

3. Invoke a local `.ps1` inside the same MXC environment. It fails with:

   ```text
   AuthorizationManager check failed.
   CategoryInfo          : SecurityError
   FullyQualifiedErrorId : UnauthorizedAccess
   ```

   Invoking the local `codex.ps1 --version` shim inside that environment fails the same way.

4. A basic MXC process-launch probe using `cmd.exe` succeeds with `MXC_OK`, so the failure occurs when PowerShell checks script authorization.

### Additional diagnostics

- A one-time diagnostic launch that supplied the host's existing `RemoteSigned` policy to the PowerShell child and removed cross-version module paths allowed the same script to run. No persistent policy or Codex configuration was changed.
- Removing the PowerShell 7 module paths alone did not fix the registry-access failure.
- When Windows PowerShell 5.1 is launched from a PowerShell 7 process, it can inherit PowerShell 7 paths in `PSModulePath`; importing modules from those paths causes additional module-loading errors. This is separate from the execution-policy registry failure.

### Expected behavior

When the host's effective policy permits a local script, PowerShell should be able to evaluate that policy and run the script inside MXC, while MXC continues enforcing its filesystem and process restrictions. Users should not need to weaken machine-wide policy or remove an otherwise functioning PowerShell installation. If MXC does not support PowerShell script execution, the CLI should report that limitation clearly.

### Related reports

- Exact same `AuthorizationManager check failed` / denied execution-policy registry read under Windows MXC in the Copilot SDK: https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/issues/2594
- Related Codex reports for PowerShell behavior inside the Windows sandbox: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/17112 and https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/17019
- Separate Codex report where a Store/MSIX `pwsh.exe` alias cannot be started by the Windows sandbox: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/18937

### Steps to reproduce on the affected installation

1. Open an existing long conversation in the Windows Codex app.
2. Scroll to the current messages at the bottom.
3. Keep the RDP viewer itself visible and connected.
4. Minimise only the Codex app window inside that desktop.
5. Restore Codex.

The app content is briefly blank/white. It then renders, but the conversation is at the top and the user must scroll back down. The duration of the white interval was not measured.

The user also tested leaving Codex restored, switching to another app inside the same remote desktop with Alt+Tab, and switching back **without minimising Codex or RDP**. The user confirmed that the chat kept its position.

This is only a workaround for switching between applications. The user specifically needs to expose the desktop to see desktop gadgets; Alt+Tab does not provide that. A subsequent user check in the same full-screen RDP desktop held Windows+comma for temporary desktop peek, then released the keys. The user confirmed: "Gadgets visible; chat position preserved." - Read-only client checks found `RemoteDesktop_SuppressWhenMinimized` absent in the checked current-user and machine 32/64-bit registry views. ### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.40934 (build 20770, prod; updater reports up to date). Windows package: 26.1013.4894.0.

### What subscription do you have?

Not specified; GPT-6.1 Sol is available to the signed-in account on both hosts.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64 desktop app connected to a Linux x86_64 remote host.

### What issue are you seeing?

In the Windows desktop app, selecting a Linux remote host and then choosing Default/Recommended in the model menu changes an explicitly selected GPT-6.1 Sol to GPT-5.6 Sol. GPT-6.1 Sol remains available.

The Linux PATH CLI was upgraded from 0.160.1 to stable 0.163.0; the user reported the same menu behavior afterward. The running remote app-server executable is releases/0.163.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/bin/codex. PC bundled CLI: 0.163.0-alpha.10.2.

The remote config.toml was verified as gpt-6.1-sol / low after a deliberate change, and later read as gpt-5.6-sol / low after the user reported choosing Recommended.

A separate fresh diagnostic app-server process (clientInfo.name=model-diagnostic) returned model/list with gpt-6.1-sol isDefault=true and gpt-5.6-sol isDefault=false. This was not a capture from the already-running desktop connection. Both cached catalogs included GPT-6.1 Sol at priority 1 and GPT-5.6 Sol at priority 6.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Connect the Windows desktop app to a Linux remote host.
2. Explicitly select GPT-6.1 Sol with low reasoning.
3. Open the model menu and select Default/Recommended.
4. Observe the selected model change to GPT-5.6 Sol.
5. Inspect remote config.toml: model is now "gpt-5.6-sol", while model_reasoning_effort remains "low".

The UI sequence above was reported by the user. Config values and installed bundle code were inspected directly. No screenshot or live desktop RPC trace was captured.

### What is the expected behavior?

Use the available server default GPT-6.1 Sol, or supply an up-to-date recommendation preset for remote hosts. Do not silently downgrade to an older bundled Sol preset when the server-default model is absent from the slider candidate list.

Suggested regression coverage: local and remote hosts, with and without dynamic presets, when GPT-6.1 Sol isDefault=true and GPT-5.6 Sol is also available.

### Additional information

Read-only inspection of the installed app.asar suggests this mechanism (minified identifiers are build-specific):

webview/assets/app-initial-5851df3f6cb1.js
- L_o supplies slider preset configuration but immediately returns null for remote hosts: if(t!==`local`)return null;
- A9a builds candidates from sliderModelsConfig.presets if supplied; otherwise it tries bundled B9a, then V9a.
- B9a contains gpt-5.6-terra:low and gpt-5.6-sol with low/medium/high/xhigh/ultra. V9a contains GPT-5.6 Terra presets. Neither fallback array includes GPT-6.1 Sol.
- P9a first tries the preferred exact model:effort ID, then a Sol candidate with matching effort, then Sol medium and other fallbacks.

webview/assets/app-primary-fe8a450b3b04.js
- The composer reads Le from Sfe (alias of L_o), then builds Mt via bRe (alias of A9a), passing sliderModelsConfig:ze.
- Its onSelectDefault callback Yn chooses fxe(Mt, jt == null ? undefined : `${jt.model}:${jt.defaultReasoningEffort}`), where jt is the isDefault model and fxe aliases P9a. It then saves the result through sn.

Likely mechanism: remote hosts receive no current slider presets, so candidates fall back to GPT-5.6 presets. GPT-6.1 Sol cannot match that candidate set, so the matching-effort Sol fallback selects GPT-5.6 Sol low. This is a code-based diagnosis, not a confirmed statement of the intended design.

Observed 2026-10-21 (Asia/Seoul). No credentials, account IDs, private host addresses, source project contents, or raw session logs are included.

items.title: Propagate authentication header failures before sending requests
items.body:
Propagate authentication header failures before sending requests

## Why

Synchronous auth header construction could silently return no credentials when managed authentication became unavailable. Callers need an error to avoid sending requests with missing or partial authentication.

## What changed

- Make `AuthProvider::add_auth_headers`, `to_auth_headers`, and auth header telemetry fallible, and propagate failures through request and WebSocket setup.
- Return a transient error when managed authentication is unavailable, and preserve network policy denials through auth error conversion.
- Retry transient MCP authentication errors while treating build errors and policy denials as terminal.
- Cancel local MCP event streams before resolving authentication so cleanup still works when credentials become unavailable.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for rejected partial authentication, async header resolution, terminal auth errors without sending requests, managed account changes, MCP retry classification, and local stream cancellation after authentication becomes unavailable.

items.title: Clarify skill usage count semantics and expose unique skill-turn counts

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI / app-server skill analytics. This request is based on source inspection of upstream main at `d34f104c22ae815fc213641b8a637c5947f14ac1` (2026-10-20), not a reproduced dashboard discrepancy.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please document the counting unit behind skill usage reports and expose a separate count of **unique turns using each skill**, alongside invocation counts.

For adoption statistics, a turn that explicitly selects a skill and subsequently reads that skill's instructions should contribute one skill-using turn. Keeping both explicit and implicit invocation events is useful for diagnostics; those events answer a different question from how many turns used the skill.

Suggested behavior:

- Preserve the existing explicit/implicit event stream.
- Document whether the report's `invocation_counts` includes both event types, and how repeated explicit invocations are treated.
- Expose a distinct `(thread_id, turn_id, skill_id)` count, or an equivalent clearly named skill-using-turn metric, without changing the meaning of the existing field.
- Label invocation counts and unique skill-using turns separately in the reporting surface. A turn using two skills should count once for each skill, while remaining one overall turn.

This request does not concern token billing, per-skill cost allocation, or task-success measurement.

### Additional information

The current separation is explicitly documented: [the OTel README](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d34f104c22ae815fc213641b8a637c5947f14ac1/codex-rs/otel/README.md#L109) says that "explicit injection and later implicit access are distinct events" and that invocation does not establish successful task completion. I am therefore filing this as a metric-definition/enhancement request, not claiming that emitting both events is a bug.

The relevant source paths are:

1. [Explicit injection emits one invocation entry per injected skill](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d34f104c22ae815fc213641b8a637c5947f14ac1/codex-rs/core/src/skills.rs#L150).
2. [Implicit shell detection maintains a separate per-turn seen set](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d34f104c22ae815fc213641b8a637c5947f14ac1/codex-rs/core/src/skills.rs#L188). Explicit injection does not populate that set.
3. [The analytics reducer deduplicates resource-backed implicit events](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d34f104c22ae815fc213641b8a637c5947f14ac1/codex-rs/analytics/src/reducer.rs#L1429), preserving the distinction from explicit events.
4. [The skill report schema](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d34f104c22ae815fc213641b8a637c5947f14ac1/codex-rs/codex-backend-openapi-models/src/models/analytics.rs#L202) exposes `skill_name`, `display_name`, `skill_ids`, and `invocation_counts`, but no unique-turn count or invocation-type breakdown. The client fetches this from [`analytics/daily-skill-usage-metrics`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d34f104c22ae815fc213641b8a637c5947f14ac1/codex-rs/backend-client/src/client/analytics.rs#L50).

A source-derived same-turn example illustrates the distinction:

| Sequence for skill S in turn T | Invocation events | Unique skill-using turns |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Explicitly inject S | 1 explicit | 1 |
| First recognized implicit read of S | +1 implicit | still 1 |
| Repeated implicit read of S | no additional implicit event | still 1 |
| Use S again in a later turn | a new invocation can be recorded | 2 |

The public repository contains the event generation and report contract, but not the backend aggregation implementation. I have not verified whether that backend already deduplicates these events, and I am not asserting that the displayed count is inflated. If `invocation_counts` already means unique skill-using turns, documenting that contract would resolve much of this ambiguity.

A focused regression/contract test covering same-turn explicit injection followed by implicit access, a second distinct skill, and a later turn would make the intended counting semantics clear.

Related but different requests: #41760 and #45357 concern exposing attributable skill events in local/OTel logs; this request concerns the meaning and presentation of aggregate usage counts.

No Codex build, inference run, or dashboard test was performed for this report.

Ordinary read-only commands, including reading an existing repository file, repeatedly exited with status 101:

```text
thread 'main' (101615) panicked at linux-sandbox/src/linux_run_main.rs:1362:17:
failed to resolve synthetic mount registry temp directory /run/user/1000/codex-tmp: No such file or directory (os error 2)
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```

The failure happened before the shell command executed. In the original conversation, the same file reads succeeded outside the sandbox. A later sandboxed read in a side conversation reproduced the same panic.

## Sequence observed

1. Work in a Codex Desktop conversation with functioning shell tools.
2. Restart the laptop between turns.
3. Continue using the conversation.
4. Normal sandboxed commands fail with the panic above because `/run/user/1000/codex-tmp` is absent.
5. In an ordinary user terminal, recreate the directory:

   ```sh
   mkdir -p -m 700 /run/user/1000/codex-tmp
   ```

6. Retry a normal sandboxed command in Codex. It succeeds immediately.

This was an observed incident, not a controlled reboot reproduction. The reboot is a plausible trigger because `/run/user/<uid>` is ephemeral, but we did not establish what originally configured or created `codex-tmp`, or independently prove when it was removed.

## Verified recovery

After directory creation, a non-escalated `exec_command` successfully ran `pwd`, inspected the directory, and read the first five lines of an existing repository Ruby file. Exit status was 0. The directory was owned by the logged-in user with mode `700`.

No repository changes, sandbox disabling, cache deletion, or app restart were needed for recovery.

## Expected behavior

Codex or the launcher responsible for configuring its private temporary directory should ensure it exists before starting the sandbox, including after reboot. If the directory cannot be initialized safely, report an actionable setup error instead of panicking and breaking all sandboxed commands.

## Source observation

The current public implementation of `synthetic_mount_registry_root()` calls `std::env::temp_dir().canonicalize()` and panics when that fails, matching the observed message:

https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/linux-sandbox/src/linux_run_main.rs

The missing parent temporary directory is encountered before registry creation. It remains unclear whether the durable fix belongs in the Desktop launcher/environment initialization or sandbox startup handling.

## Related report

https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/16970 describes stale/deleted `~/.codex/tmp/arg0` helper paths. This report has a different failure point: the sandbox executable starts, then panics resolving its temporary directory. Recreating the directory, rather than regenerating helper executables, fixes this incident.

Could maintainers confirm which component owns initialization of this directory and whether a fix is planned or already included in a newer Desktop build?

items.title: [macOS Desktop] App update leaves primary host’s app-managed server outdated in a two-host SSH setup

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Desktop app bundle inspected: `26.1013.40934` (build `20770`, installed as `ChatGPT.app`). Its bundled CLI reports `0.163.0-alpha.10.2`. The separately installed Homebrew CLI reports `0.163.0`.

Both macOS desktop clients and both standalone CLIs had been updated before investigating. The bundled and standalone CLI versions are listed separately; this report does not assume they must have identical version strings.

### What subscription do you have?

Not supplied in this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Two macOS hosts: a MacBook and a Mac Mini, configured to connect to one another through the desktop app's SSH connections. The Mac Mini execution host reports `Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm`.

### What issue are you seeing?

**Possible app-server lifecycle/update bug: updating the desktop app on the primary host does not reliably replace the already-running app-managed server on that same host.** In this two-host SSH setup, updating both desktop apps and both standalone CLIs left older app-server processes running. The primary/local server is a central part of this report, not just the remote SSH server.

The primary host's local app-managed server survived multiple full app quits and restarts and remained outdated. Manually terminating that process was required to get an updated server. There was no local-server restart action apparent in Settings. The user reports similar upgrade-related problems on at least three previous occasions and performs upgrades when no session is actively running a query.

The CLI daemon restart command could not manage the app-launched server:

```text
$ codex app-server daemon restart
Error: app server is running but is not managed by codex app-server daemon
```

#### Measured evidence from the remote host

Before recovery, `codex app-server daemon version` reported the following relevant fields:

```json
{
  "status": "running",
  "managedCodexVersion": null,
  "cliVersion": "0.163.0",
  "appServerVersion": "0.160.0"
}
```

The old process had started on October 5 and was still running on October 20. Its command line was:

```text
codex -c features.code_mode_host=true app-server --listen unix://
```

Its executable was still associated with:

```text
/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/codex/0.160.0.upgrading/bin/codex
```

A newly launched `codex app-server proxy` was connecting to that older server even though the installed CLI was already `0.163.0`.

After manually terminating the remote server, the connection briefly dropped. With the desktop client still open, a replacement appeared automatically and reported `appServerVersion: 0.163.0`. It still had `managedCodexVersion: null`.

The stale primary/local server was also updated by manually terminating it. The exact old primary/local server version was not recorded in this report; the `0.160.0` to `0.163.0` measurements above belong to the remote host.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed workflow; not yet reduced to a clean-install reproduction:

1. Set up the desktop app on two Macs and configure SSH connections between them. Use the primary desktop client to work on the other host.
2. Allow the app/SSH workflow to start its persistent app servers.
3. With no query actively running, update the desktop client on the primary host and update the separately installed CLI. Update the client and CLI on the other host as well.
4. Fully quit and reopen the primary desktop app, and reconnect through the SSH workflow.
5. Compare installed versions with the actual running app-server versions on each host.
6. Observe that the primary host's local server can remain on an older version despite updating and fully quitting/restarting that app. The remote server can also remain stale, as measured above.
7. Attempt `codex app-server daemon restart`; it refuses because the server is not managed by that CLI daemon facility.

### What is the expected behavior?

The desktop app should reconcile the app servers it launches or reuses with the runtime expected by the updated app, on the primary host as well as SSH-connected hosts.

At a safe point after an update, it should either restart the affected server automatically or provide a visible, supported restart/update action. If another connected client prevents replacement, the UI should explain that and provide a supported path forward. Users should not need to identify and kill detached processes to finish a normal update.

This is not a request for an SSH reconnect to install or upgrade software on other machines. Both apps and CLIs were already updated; the missing step was activating the appropriate installed runtime in the persistent server processes.

### Impact and uncertainty

An updated client can continue talking to an outdated server indefinitely. As app-server APIs and tool capabilities change, this risks incompatibilities and leaves server fixes inactive despite the user having completed the normal upgrade routine.

This investigation began after remote connector/tool discovery failed with:

```text
unsupported call: tool_searchtool_search_tool
```

That error persisted after the measured remote server was updated, so this report does **not** claim the stale server caused that particular tool failure or that restarting resolves it. The confirmed issue is stale running servers and the lack of an apparent supported local recovery path.

### Related reports

- #32983 — previous server remains running after an update (Linux/CLI remote-control case).
- #46468 — CLI update leaves an old server running while daemon update/restart refuse recovery (npm/WSL case).
- #49418 — automatic updates for CLI-managed app servers (Windows feature request).

This report adds the desktop-managed macOS case with two SSH-connected hosts, especially the primary host's own server surviving app updates and full quits.

items.title: Durable host WebSocket (wss://codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com/) never establishes and loops on open_timeout / 1006 in the Windows desktop app

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

items.body:
### Summary

Two separate problems on Codex desktop for Windows. They have different causes.

- **A. `server_overloaded` returned for ~40–50% of turns** while quota was at 58–60% of the 5-hour window.
  Reproduces on the CLI as well, so it is a service-side capacity signal rather than a client problem.
- **B. The durable ("Long-lived") host WebSocket never connects.** Every attempt dies at exactly 15.0 s
  with close code `1006` / `failureReason=open_timeout`. It dials **directly**, bypassing the system proxy,
  to a DNS answer that does not belong to Cloudflare/OpenAI, and stays in `SynSent`. Switching the egress
  exit changes nothing, because the connection never uses the proxy.

### Environment

- Codex desktop **26.1013.4894.0**, Microsoft Store MSIX (`OpenAI.Codex_26.1013.4894.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0`, SignatureKind = Store)
- codex-cli **0.163.0-alpha.10.2**
- Windows 11 x64 (10.0.26100), zh-CN, timezone Asia/Shanghai (UTC+08:00)
- ChatGPT Plus, auth mode `chatgpt` (`codex login status` → "Logged in using ChatGPT")
- Network: Windows system (WinINET) proxy; direct HTTP access is filtered in this network

### Defect A — `server_overloaded`

70 failed turns between 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-20, of which 69 are
`Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.` (`codex_error_info: server_overloaded`)
and 1 is `workspace routing discovery unauthorized (401)`. 269 turns succeeded in the same period.

| Date (CST) | Failed turns |
|---|---|
| 2026-10-14 | 1 |
| 2026-10-15 | 1 |
| 2026-10-19 | 28 |
| 2026-10-20 | 40 |

Models among failures: `gpt-6.1-sol` 32, `gpt-6-astra` 29, `codex-auto-review` 3, `gpt-5.6-luna` 2,
`gpt-5.6-sol` 2, `gpt-6-luna` 1, `gpt-6-sol` 1.

Quota at the failing turns never exceeded 60% of the 5-hour window (14% weekly).

**Reproduces outside the desktop app:** `codex exec --skip-git-repo-check -m gpt-6.1-sol "Reply with the single word: OK"`,
ten consecutive runs on 2026-10-20 20:47–20:54 CST — runs 1–9 succeeded, run 10 failed after 17.5 s with
`ERROR: Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.`

`codex doctor` reports `websocket connected (HTTP 101 Switching Protocols)`, `connect timeout 15000 ms`,
and both the inference and CDN endpoints reachable, so Defect A is not a connectivity issue.

### Defect B — durable WebSocket never establishes

The endpoint is defined in `resources/app.asar`:

```js
var uue = `wss://codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com/`;
function lb(e){ return { id: i.Ai, display_name: `Long-lived`, kind: `local`, websocket_url: uue } }
this.durableThreadHostConfig = lb({ ... })
```

One attempt from the desktop log (no credentials present):

```
13:08:39.434Z info  [AppServerConnection] Starting app-server connection hostId=durable
13:08:39.445Z info  [AppServerConnection] Transport start success connectionId=2
13:08:54.449Z error [AppServerConnection] websocket_error  hostKind=durable
                    message="WebSocket was closed before the connection was established"
13:08:54.449Z info  [AppServerConnection] closed  code=1006  failureReason=open_timeout
```

That is 15.004 s — the client's own 15,000 ms connect timeout. This repeats continuously
(457 attempts on 2026-10-20, `reconnect_failed` 478 times), while the pubsub transport on the same machine
connects normally and `codex doctor`'s own WebSocket handshake returns 101.

**It is not the egress.** Two different proxy exits, app restarted before each phase:

| Phase | Window (CST) | Duration | Attempts | Failures | Per minute |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A (exit 1) | 21:06:34 – 21:20:51 | 14.3 min | 27 | 25 | 1.75 |
| B (exit 2, app restarted 21:20:38) | 21:20:51 – 21:35:26 | 14.6 min | 26 | 27 | 1.85 |

**What the process is actually doing:**

```
local DNS   codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com -> <addresses not belonging to Cloudflare/OpenAI>
process     ChatGPT.exe (Electron main)     -> <that address>:443   state = SynSent, repeating
```

The Electron main process opens the socket itself instead of handing it to the Windows system proxy.
The SYN goes to an address that never answers, so after 15 s the client aborts with 1006. No request is
ever sent — which is also why the interesting question "is auth attached before or after" cannot apply here.

**The host itself is fine when the proxy is used.** Hand-rolled probe through the system proxy
(HTTP CONNECT → TLS → `Upgrade: websocket`):

| Target | CONNECT | TLS | Certificate | Upgrade response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com` | 200 / 23 ms | TLS 1.3 / 327 ms | CN=chatgpt.com, GTS WE1 | 403 in 106 ms |
| `chatgpt.com` | 200 / 1 ms | TLS 1.3 / 264 ms | CN=chatgpt.com, GTS WE1 | 403 in 100 ms |
| `ws.chatgpt.com` | 200 / 0 ms | TLS 1.3 / 347 ms | CN=ws.chatgpt.com, GTS WE1 | 404 in 577 ms |

The 403 carries `Server: cloudflare` and a `CF-RAY` header — Cloudflare bot management rejecting an
unauthenticated client, not a network block. The point is the 106 ms: the host answers immediately,
while the app never gets an answer at all.

### Requested

1. Does the connection with `hostId=durable` (`wss://codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com/`) honour the Windows
   system proxy? Here it dials directly from the Electron main process. On a network that requires a proxy
   and where direct DNS is filtered, durable / Long-lived threads can never work.
2. If it is not proxy-aware today, is that intended? If not, this is the bug.
3. Separately: is `server_overloaded` expected at 40–50% of turns with quota near 60%, and is there a
   distinction between desktop and CLI routing that would explain the different rates?

### Notes

- Session identifiers, full transcripts and exact log excerpts were provided privately through the
  official support conversation and are intentionally omitted here.
- Happy to provide additional log slices or run any diagnostic you suggest.

items.title: Avoid panics after background compaction fails before a checkpoint
items.body:
Avoid panics after background compaction fails before a checkpoint

## Why

Polling a failed background compaction consumes the closed oneshot receiver.
Keeping that receiver in session state can cause a later await to panic instead
of falling back to foreground compaction.

## What changed

Remove the receiver from session state before polling it, restoring it only when
its result is still pending. Discard closed receivers so compaction can fall back
normally.

## Testing

Add a regression scenario where background compaction fails before the next
checkpoint and automatic compaction falls back successfully.

items.body:
### Summary

The actual Codex executable used by my Windows Desktop installation still reproduces the terminal SSE failure-handling defect described in #43140.

When a server sends `response.failed` but keeps the connection open, the client loses the original error and eventually reports:

```text
stream disconnected before completion: idle timeout waiting for SSE
```

This report adds evidence from **codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.10.2**, bundled with a Desktop installation whose configured updater reports it is up to date.

### Environment

- Windows 11
- Codex Desktop: **26.1013.40934**, build **20770**
- Release channel: **prod**
- Actual running core, verified with its executable's `--version`: **codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.10.2**

### Reproduction

An independent Python harness ran the installed executable against a loopback HTTP SSE fixture. Each case used a fresh, isolated configuration and credential directory, no live model inference, and no account credentials. The model-provider URL and the auxiliary ChatGPT catalog base URL both pointed to the fixture. Recorded requests contained no Authorization header.

The test configured:

```toml
wire_api = "responses"
requires_openai_auth = false
request_max_retries = 0
stream_max_retries = 0
stream_idle_timeout_ms = 800
```

The fixture returned HTTP 200 with `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and sent:

```text
event: response.failed
data: {"type":"response.failed","response":{"id":"resp_loopback_diagnostic","status":"failed","error":{"code":"server_error","message":"LOCAL_SSE_TERMINAL_FAILURE_TEST"}}}

```

Three cases were tested:

1. Send that event, then close the connection.
2. Send the identical event, but leave the connection open.
3. Send response headers only and leave the connection open.

### Sanitized measured results

The following is an allowlisted extract of the local test output. Timing measures emission of the user-facing error after the fixture sends its event or headers, not total process exit time.

```json
{
  "core_version": "0.163.0-alpha.10.2",
  "configured_idle_timeout_ms": 800,
  "results": [
    {
      "case": "failure_eof",
      "original_error_in_user_output": true,
      "idle_timeout_in_user_output": false,
      "original_error_in_debug_log": true,
      "error_emission_delay_seconds_rounded": 0.000,
      "exit_code": 1,
      "harness_timeout": false
    },
    {
      "case": "failure_hold_open",
      "original_error_in_user_output": false,
      "idle_timeout_in_user_output": true,
      "original_error_in_debug_log": true,
      "error_emission_delay_seconds_rounded": 0.813,
      "exit_code": 1,
      "harness_timeout": false
    },
    {
      "case": "silent",
      "original_error_in_user_output": false,
      "idle_timeout_in_user_output": true,
      "original_error_in_debug_log": false,
      "error_emission_delay_seconds_rounded": 0.812,
      "exit_code": 1,
      "harness_timeout": false
    }
  ]
}
```

In the held-open case, tracing captured the synthetic original error, but the CLI emitted:

```json
{"type":"error","message":"stream disconnected before completion: idle timeout waiting for SSE"}
{"type":"turn.failed","error":{"message":"stream disconnected before completion: idle timeout waiting for SSE"}}
```

The fixture intentionally did not provide a model catalog, so the CLI also emitted a fallback-model-metadata warning in every case. The test covers transport/error handling, not model inference.

### Source inspection and expected behavior

The matching [release source](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0-alpha.10.2/codex-rs/codex-api/src/sse/responses.rs) still stores most parsed errors in `response_error` and continues polling. EOF returns that saved error, while the idle-timeout branch sends a new timeout error. The existing immediate-return exceptions do not cover the synthetic `server_error` above.

Please treat terminal `response.failed` as terminal immediately, preserving its classified error. The later lifetime of the HTTP connection should not obscure an already-received terminal failure.

### Production context and evidence boundary

The investigation followed repeated stalls during ordinary PowerPoint editing in a long-running Desktop conversation. Production logs included response-body decoding failures and an SSE idle timeout.

Those production logs did not retain the raw terminal SSE event. Therefore, this report **does not claim that the reproduced defect caused that particular production timeout**. The silent control demonstrates why the final timeout text alone cannot settle that question.

Editing existing documents and invoking local file tools are normal product usage. Users need actionable errors without having to debug the streaming implementation.

### Requested resolution

- Confirm whether this defect remains in the Desktop-bundled runtime.
- Identify the official release that fixes it.
- Preserve terminal failure details promptly and provide privacy-conscious error diagnostics.
- Do not treat increasing the idle timeout as a fix for this reproduction.

Related: #43140. Please consolidate with that issue if preferred.

This report deliberately excludes personal paths, usernames, session identifiers, production request IDs, network addresses, conversation contents, and credentials. The response ID and error marker shown above are synthetic test values.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.40934, build 20770. Read from the installed macOS app's Info.plist, not the About dialog.

### What subscription do you have?

Pro Lite. The account usage tool returned planType `prolite`.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 27.0.1, Apple Silicon.
`uname -mprs`: `Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm`
Timezone: Asia/Jerusalem.

### What issue are you seeing?

A local in-chat heartbeat scheduled for one execution actually ran again the following day. This is an execution problem, not only an incorrect schedule label.

The saved definition contained:
- kind: `heartbeat`
- status: `ACTIVE`
- schedule: `FREQ=DAILY;COUNT=1;BYHOUR=15;BYMINUTE=30;BYSECOND=0`

Its prompt explicitly limited the work to October 19, 2026 and said it was one execution, not recurring work.

The conversation log contains two heartbeat deliveries for the same automation:
- First delivery: October 19, 2026 at `12:30:30.821Z`, or 15:30:30 Asia/Jerusalem.
- Duplicate delivery: October 20, 2026 at `12:30:04.695Z`, or 15:30:04 Asia/Jerusalem.

The last saved configuration update before those deliveries was October 19 at `07:21:56.010Z`, before the first execution. The inspected conversation contains no automation update between the two deliveries.

The first execution completed its requested work. On the second execution, the assistant recognized that the work was already complete and took no deployment action. The automation still had ACTIVE status and the same one-run limit when inspected after that duplicate.

A second completed one-run heartbeat also remained ACTIVE. We have not observed a duplicate from that second timer. Both timers were explicitly paused after this investigation.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence, not a new controlled reproduction:
1. Create or update a local heartbeat in an existing chat with the daily schedule and COUNT=1 shown above.
2. Specify one particular date and say that the task must execute only once.
3. Leave the app available for the intended execution. Let the task complete.
4. Do not edit or reactivate the automation after that execution.
5. Observe another heartbeat delivery at the same local time on the next day.

For a safe regression test, use a harmless prompt that only reports the current time. Do not use deployment work.

### What is the expected behavior?

COUNT=1 should permit exactly one scheduled delivery. After that occurrence, no later heartbeat should be delivered without an explicit schedule reset or reactivation. The app should expose the completed state clearly.

### Additional information

Read-only inspection of the installed app bundle provides a possible explanation:
- In `.vite/build/src-DsLVGakC.js`, `YF()` accepts a daily COUNT=1 rule without DTSTART when hour and minute are present. Its local-calendar branch calls `gI()`, which returns the next daily occurrence. That branch does not track whether the single occurrence has already been consumed.
- In `.vite/build/main-CLu1A25j.js`, `ol()` has an explicit stop condition for due one-run `cron` automations. That condition excludes `heartbeat`. The heartbeat path can call the next-occurrence calculation again.

This is static inspection of the installed build. No modified app, instrumented scheduler run, or separate minimal reproduction was used. The duplicate delivery itself is directly recorded in the conversation log.

Related: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/19094 describes a COUNT=1 display problem and explicitly does not establish repeated execution. This report adds evidence of an actual second execution.

Please test one-run heartbeat completion across daily dispatch, app restart, and configuration reload.

Private deployment instructions, project identifiers, conversation IDs, credentials, and raw logs are omitted. No feedback upload was performed.

### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex desktop on Windows, Dots, and Dot-delegated Codex tasks. Observed October 20, 2026.

### What feature would you like to see?

**Let users explicitly grant Dots and their delegated Codex tasks the local capabilities needed to finish work: CLI execution, selected files and projects, local services, and configured MCP integrations—with clear scopes, approvals, and reliable result retrieval.**

I use a Dot to coordinate engineering and automation work on my connected PC. I want to describe an outcome once and let the Dot execute it, or delegate it to a normal local Codex task and collect the result. Today, capabilities differ depending on how the task was created, and the permission selector does not make those differences clear.

Please provide:

1. **An explicit execution target:** choose the connected computer and whether to create a native local Codex task or a cloud-backed task using local execution.
2. **User-configurable capability grants:** select permitted CLI tools/commands, working directories, network destinations/local services, and supported MCP integrations. Offer task-scoped and reusable grants, with revocation and applicable administrator policies.
3. **Consistent delegated access:** show which approved capabilities a child task receives. If access cannot carry over, explain why and offer a supported approval path rather than silently omitting tools.
4. **Supported authenticated integrations:** let authorized tasks use configured integrations through normal credential handling, without requiring the agent to extract secrets or recreate authentication manually.
5. **A complete coordination loop:** reliably create, wait for, read, continue, and stop local Codex tasks from a Dot, including support for current thread formats.
6. **Effective-access diagnostics:** distinguish cloud coordination from command execution location, and show actual filesystem/network permissions, exposed tools, connection status, and actionable failures.

**Comparison with Grok Bot**

Grok Bot documents using a terminal, files, and connected tools on its persistent computer, plus executing commands on a user's local computer when enabled and approved under the local-computer policy. Its engineering guide describes creating agents, reading transcripts, and sending follow-ups:

- https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/computer-and-apps
- https://x.ai/bot/guides/grok-bot-for-engineering

I want that kind of complete, permission-controlled delegation experience with Dots + Codex. The request is for users to configure access deliberately and have the selected capabilities work consistently across delegation, while preserving enforced policies.

### Additional information

**Observed example—not the scope of the feature request**

We tested a local T3 Code MCP integration as one concrete example of the broader access gap:

- A normal local Codex chat could call the integration and successfully create a harmless conversation and read its reply.
- A Dot-created cloud-backed task could run PowerShell on the connected Windows PC but had no callable tools for that configured integration.
- A sandboxed local HTTP request initially encountered a socket-permission denial. With Full access selected, a later request reached the service. Its 401 response came from a raw unauthenticated request, so it did not establish a broken existing MCP login.
- A fresh cloud-backed task successfully created a normal local Codex diagnostic task using the supported desktop tool.
- The local child reported **83 exposed T3 tools**. This was inventory-only; it did not test connectivity.
- The cloud-backed parent could not retrieve the child's result, reporting unavailable hosts. The Dot additionally reported that its reader rejected the newer thread format. A normal local Codex chat successfully read the completed result.

This is not a claim that Dots cannot execute any local commands: they did in this test. The gap is consistent access to the user's selected environment and integrations, plus reliable follow-through. The underlying cause of each failure has not been established.

**Desired acceptance test:** I authorize a Dot to use a selected connected PC and its approved tools, request a harmless CLI/integration task, and receive the verified result without manually opening another chat or relaying messages.

Related reports with narrower or overlapping symptoms: #50544 (local executor/local-thread workflows), #53136 (local MCP exposure on macOS), and #54403 (Dot CLI network/authentication workflow). This request focuses on an explicit, user-configurable capability and delegation model across Dots + Codex; it does not assert a common root cause.

- Multiple older Ariana workspaces marked "Deactivated"

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Installed package: `openai-codex-desktop 26.1013.40934-1` (package-manager version; the About dialog was not captured).

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

```text
Observation date:  2026-10-20
OS:               Arch Linux / Omarchy
Kernel:           7.2.8-9-omarchy, x86_64
Hyprland:         0.56.2-4
Backend:          Native Wayland (--ozone-platform=wayland)
CPU:              Intel Core Ultra 7 255H
RAM:              Approximately 15 GiB
Storage:          Encrypted NVMe
Home filesystem:  Btrfs with compress=zstd:3
Display setup:    Reproduces with one monitor as well as multiple monitors
```

### What issue are you seeing?

The Linux desktop client repeatedly rewrites its entire global-state JSON and backup at approximately **9–10 saves per second**, despite the avatar being disabled.

During successive state comparisons, `electron-avatar-overlay-bounds` was the only section observed changing. Its coordinates oscillate between two positions while the display ID and display bounds remain unchanged.

Measured impact:

- **~91–94 MiB/s** attributed to the local Electron main process.
- **~21 MiB/s** of whole-device NVMe writes during a separate simultaneous measurement.
- **~92% of one CPU core** consumed by the main process during another short sample.

My coding projects execute on a remote VPS. These measurements concern the **local desktop Electron main process**, not the remote execution environment.

#### 1. Avatar is disabled, but its saved coordinates oscillate

The saved setting is:

```json
"electron-avatar-overlay-open": false
```

Hyprland lists only the main ChatGPT window as mapped; no avatar window is listed.

Ten comparisons of successive parsed state snapshots found:

```text
Changed section: electron-avatar-overlay-bounds
Changed in:      8 of 10 comparisons
```

Subsequent snapshots showed this alternating geometry:

```text
Sample A:
  x: 679
  y: 1026

Sample B:
  x: 1920
  y: 995
```

Both retain:

```text
displayId: 71
displayBounds:
  x: 1920
  y: 0
  width: 1800
  height: 1125

placement: top-start
isFreelyPositioned: false
snapPosition: null
```

The corresponding entries in `byDisplayId` and `byResolution` also update.

These coordinate samples were collected with multiple monitors, but **the problem also occurs with only one monitor**. Multiple monitors are not a necessary condition for reproducing it.

This suggests repeated position reconciliation, but the responsible call stack has not been captured. **Hyprland involvement is a hypothesis, not an established cause.**

#### 2. Each update rewrites the complete state and backup

Affected files:

```text
~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json
~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json.bak
```

Each file was approximately **5,057,744 bytes / 4.82 MiB**.

Sanitized inotify/process-counter output:

```text
Observation window:                         5.00 seconds
Main-process write_bytes increase:          463.9 MiB
IN_CLOSE_WRITE on global-state temp files:  96 events
IN_MOVED_TO on primary/backup destinations: 96 events
```

A separate observation distinguished the final destinations:

```text
Observation window:                  3.32 seconds
Primary-state atomic replacements:   31
Backup-state atomic replacements:    31
```

This is consistent with approximately **9–10 full primary-plus-backup saves per second**.

Most of the payload is unrelated cached data. Two large fields under `electron-persisted-atom-state` were:

| Field | Serialized bytes |
| --- | ---: |
| `mcp-server-tools-cache-v2` | 3,300,969 |
| `mcp-extension-sidebar-catalog` | 1,159,543 |

Neither field changed during the sampled comparisons.

#### 3. Process versus device write measurements

A separate simultaneous five-second measurement recorded:

```text
Main-process /proc/<pid>/io write_bytes:   90.88 MiB/s
Whole-NVMe /sys/block/nvme0n1/stat writes:  20.83 MiB/s
```

A per-thread three-second observation attributed approximately **23 MiB/s each** to four `libuv-worker` threads. Another short sample measured approximately **92% of one CPU core** for the main process.

**Measurement caveats:**

- Process write counters are not equivalent to device-level writes.
- Whole-device counters include other applications.
- Neither measures internal SSD NAND writes.
- Compression and buffering may affect the difference.
- The fraction of CPU consumption caused by this loop has not been profiled.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is an **existing-profile observation**, not yet a clean-profile minimal reproducer.

1. Run the desktop client in the environment above. The problem occurs with either one monitor or multiple monitors.
2. Confirm `electron-avatar-overlay-open` is `false`.
3. Check mapped windows using `hyprctl clients -j`.
4. Sample parsed `electron-avatar-overlay-bounds` values without modifying the file.
5. Monitor temporary-file close events and atomic replacements in `~/.codex` using inotify.
6. Compare `/proc/<main-pid>/io` counters over several seconds.
7. Separately measure whole-device writes to avoid treating process counters as physical SSD writes.

The observations were collected read-only, with the application running normally. This was **not a controlled idle benchmark**.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Disabling the avatar should not leave an overlay-position loop repeatedly updating persisted geometry.
- Position reconciliation should converge rather than alternate indefinitely.
- Frequent geometry changes should not rewrite megabytes of unrelated caches and a full backup on every update.
- Persistence should be appropriately throttled, deduplicated, or separated by data type.

### Additional information

Related: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/51288 — same full-state/backup amplification mechanism, but apparently a different trigger and substantially lower frequency. This report adds rapid geometry oscillation with the avatar disabled, including reproduction with a single monitor; it is not a claim that the two triggers have the same root cause.

Investigation limits:

- Restart behavior, XWayland, another compositor, and a clean profile have not yet been tested.
- No application code, configuration, or state files were modified during diagnostic collection.
- No stack trace identifying the update source was captured.
- Raw global-state contents are intentionally omitted because they contain private data.

Could maintainers investigate the disabled-overlay geometry update path and whether coordinate reconciliation can repeatedly trigger full-state persistence under Wayland?

The shortcut should only copy the selected screenshot to the macOS clipboard. With Appshots Hotkey=None, the app should not initiate an attachment or show an attachment error. The screenshot should remain available to paste.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### Environment

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| App | ChatGPT desktop app (Windows, MSIX `OpenAI.Codex_26.1013.4894.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0`) |
| Bundled app-server | `codex 0.163.0-alpha.10.2` (windows-x86_64) |
| OS | Windows 11 10.0.26200 x64 |
| Proxy | Clash Verge Rev (mihomo core); Windows **system proxy** enabled (`ProxyEnable=1`, `127.0.0.1:7897`); TUN **not** enabled |
| Network | DNS poisoning present: `chatgpt.com` resolves to random forged IPs |

### Problem

After `remoteControl/enable`, the desktop app also opens a WebSocket to the `hostId=durable` ("Long-lived") host:

```js
// app.asar — hardcoded, no config override
var uue = `wss://codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com/`;
function lb(e){ return { id: i.Ai, display_name: `Long-lived`, kind: `local`, websocket_url: uue } }
```

It is issued from the Electron **main process** using the Node `ws` package (not the Chromium network stack), and as a result:

1. it does **not** read the Windows system proxy (WinINET / `ProxyEnable` + `ProxyServer`), even though the HTTP client inside the app-server does;
2. it does **not** read `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY`, even though `codex.exe` in the same process tree does (see the A/B test below);
3. the URL is hardcoded and there is **no setting** to override it.

On any network that requires a proxy — in particular "system proxy on, TUN off", which is the default setup for a very large number of users in mainland China — this connection fails deterministically.

### Reproduction

1. Enable the Windows system proxy (pointing at a local HTTP proxy). Do **not** enable TUN.
2. Use a network where `chatgpt.com` is DNS-poisoned (or any network that requires a proxy).
3. Launch the ChatGPT desktop app, open Settings → Connections → Control this computer, enable "Allow connection".
4. Watch the desktop app log
   (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\OpenAI.Codex_2p2nqsd0c76g0\LocalCache\Local\Codex\Logs\`):

```
[AppServerConnection] app_server_connection.websocket_error connectionId=58 errorCode=unknown
  hostKind=durable message="WebSocket was closed before the connection was established" transport=websocket
[AppServerConnection] app_server_connection.closed code=1006 connectionId=58 failureReason=open_timeout
[AppServerConnection] app_server_connection.reconnect_scheduled baseDelayMs=20000 reconnectAttempt=57
```

5. In parallel, `Get-NetTCPConnection` on the main process shows a **direct** connection to a public IP stuck in `SynSent` (the DNS-poisoned address) instead of the local proxy:

```
RemoteAddress    RemotePort  State
127.0.0.1        7897        Established      <- Chromium traffic goes through the proxy
199.16.158.190   443         SynSent          <- long-lived WS connects directly, hits a forged IP
```

### A/B test: the app-server *does* honor proxy env vars

Same machine, same subscription, one variable changed at a time, using `codex remote-control --no-daemon` and looking for `connected to app-server remote control websocket` in the log:

| Group | `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` | Extra flag | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | set | — | ✅ `connected to app-server remote control websocket` |
| E | set | — | ✅ reproduces A |
| B | set | `-c features.respect_system_proxy=true` | ❌ `Error: Remote control is enabled on <name> but the connection is errored.` |
| C | cleared | — | ❌ `os error 10060` (WSAETIMEDOUT) |
| D | cleared | `-c features.network_proxy=true -c network.proxy_url=...` | ❌ `os error 10060` |

So the Rust app-server **does** honor `HTTP_PROXY`, while the main-process WebSocket does not — inconsistent proxy behavior inside the same app/process tree.

Two further observations:

- `features.respect_system_proxy=true` (which reads the Windows system proxy from the registry) makes the app-server WS fail outright with `connection is errored`; the system-proxy path appears to be broken for the WS transport.
- `network.proxy_url` / `network.socks_url` (`features.network_proxy`) only apply to network policy for **sandboxed commands**; they do not cover the app-server's own long-lived connections.

### The endpoint itself works (so this is not a server-side problem)

WS upgrade handshake through the local proxy:

```
$ curl -x http://127.0.0.1:7897 \
    -H 'Connection: Upgrade' -H 'Upgrade: websocket' \
    -H 'Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13' -H 'Sec-WebSocket-Key: <random>' \
    -H 'Origin: https://chatgpt.com' \
    https://codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com/

User-Agent: (none)                         -> HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
User-Agent: node                           -> HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
User-Agent: codex-desktop/26.1013.4894.0   -> HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
User-Agent: ChatGPT/26.1013.4894.0         -> HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
```

As soon as the request goes through the proxy with an acceptable User-Agent, the handshake succeeds — the server and the network egress are fine.

### Isolation: after fixing the proxy env vars, the toggle works but this channel still does not

This pins the problem precisely to the connection described here:

```
# after setting user-level HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY and restarting the app
Settings -> Connections -> Control this computer -> "Allow connection"  =>  ON, pairing QR dialog shown  OK
desktop log                                                                   =>  os error 10060 gone,
                                                                                 "connected to rendezvous"  OK

# but the long-lived channel is still connecting directly
codex.exe (app-server) sockets     =>  127.0.0.1:7897  Established        OK
Electron main process "durable"    =>  199.16.158.190:443  SynSent        still direct
```

In other words: the toggle itself is backed by the app-server tunnel (now working), but the channel the **cloud uses to call back into this machine** — issued by the Electron main process — is never taken over by the proxy. **"Allow connection" being on does not mean a remote session can actually be established.**

### Expected behavior (suggestions)

1. Honor `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` / `ALL_PROXY` for WebSockets opened by the desktop app main process, consistent with the app-server.
2. At minimum honor the Windows system proxy (WinINET), so the very common "system proxy only" setup works.
3. Provide a configurable endpoint override (e.g. `CODEX_CLOUD_BACKEND_URL` or a settings entry) for self-hosted gateways / enterprise environments.
4. Fix `features.respect_system_proxy`, which currently breaks the app-server WS when enabled.

### Impact

In mainland China and any other "proxy required, system proxy only, TUN off" environment, the desktop app's cloud long-lived connection is unavailable, so **remote control sessions initiated from a phone may fail to establish** even though the "Allow connection" toggle turns on and the device shows as online.

### Paths for further investigation

```
Desktop app logs:
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\OpenAI.Codex_2p2nqsd0c76g0\LocalCache\Local\Codex\Logs\<YYYY>\<MM>\<DD>\codex-desktop-*.log

Codex CLI binary shipped with the desktop app (copied into the user profile):
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\bin\<hash>\codex.exe
```

---

*A full local investigation with all raw log excerpts, socket dumps and the A/B test matrix is also available at
https://github.com/Kirito14IT/chatgpt-codex-windows-remote-control-proxy-fix (contains one-click diagnostic scripts).*
